title: AI and ML Fundamentals
description: Core machine learning vocabulary, evaluation metrics, and model behavior.

cards.definition: Broad field of building systems that perform tasks requiring human-like intelligence
Subset of AI where models learn patterns from data instead of following explicit rules
ML using multi-layer neural networks to learn representations from large amounts of data
Layers of connected nodes (neurons) whose weights are adjusted during training
Learning from labeled input-output examples, such as classification and regression
Finding structure in unlabeled data, such as clustering or dimensionality reduction
An agent learns by taking actions and receiving rewards or penalties
Training with a small labeled dataset plus a large unlabeled one
Predicting a discrete category or label
Predicting a continuous numeric value
Grouping similar unlabeled data points together (e.g., k-means)
Data used to fit the model's parameters
Data used to tune hyperparameters and compare model versions
Held-out data used to estimate performance on unseen data
Model learns training data too closely, including noise, and performs poorly on new data
Model is too simple to capture the underlying pattern and performs poorly even on training data
High bias means underfitting; high variance means overfitting; the goal is to balance them

example.text: A property firm builds models to predict apartment rents. A simple version that uses only square footage misses badly on both training and test listings. A very complex version scores almost perfectly on training listings but poorly on new ones, because it memorized quirks of individual buildings. The team ships a middle version that does about equally well on both.

cards.definition: An input variable used by a model to make predictions
Creating, transforming, or selecting input variables to improve model performance

example.text: A gym chain wants to predict which members will cancel. Its raw data is sign-up dates plus a log of every check-in. In SageMaker Data Wrangler, an analyst turns these into new columns: months as a member, visits in the last 30 days, and days since the last visit. A model trained on those columns predicts cancellations much better than one trained on the raw log.

cards.definition: A setting chosen before training (e.g., learning rate, number of layers), not learned from data
Values the model learns during training
Measures the error between predictions and actual values; training works to minimize it
Iterative optimization that adjusts weights to reduce the loss
Using a trained model to generate predictions on new inputs
Of all predicted positives, the fraction that are truly positive: TP / (TP + FP)
Of all actual positives, the fraction the model correctly identifies: TP / (TP + FN)
Fraction of all predictions that are correct
Harmonic mean of precision and recall; useful when classes are imbalanced
Table of true vs. predicted classes showing TP, FP, TN, and FN counts

example.text: A clinic builds a model in SageMaker Canvas to flag patients likely to miss appointments. Overall accuracy looks fine at 90 percent, but the confusion matrix under Advanced metrics shows that of 200 patients who actually missed, the model flagged only 60. Those 140 false negatives would get no reminder call, so the clinic rebuilds the model with more no-show examples before using it.

cards.definition: Reusing knowledge from a model pretrained on one task to speed up learning on a related task

example.text: A furniture recycler wants to sort photos of donated items into sofas, tables, chairs and lamps, but has only 300 labeled photos of each. Instead of training from scratch, the team picks a pretrained image classification model in SageMaker JumpStart, which already recognizes general shapes and textures. It trains that model further on its own photos from Amazon S3 and gets an accurate sorter from little data and short training.

cards.definition: Change in the statistical distribution of input data after deployment

example.text: A food-delivery app predicts delivery times with a model trained mostly on city orders. After the app expands into rural towns, the data quality check in SageMaker Model Monitor flags that incoming trip distances are far longer than in the training baseline. Distance still affects delivery time the same way, but the model is seeing inputs it rarely saw in training, so the team retrains it with rural orders.

cards.definition: Change in the relationship between inputs and the target after deployment

example.text: A retailer's fraud model checks the same purchase signals as always, and SageMaker Model Monitor shows the incoming data still matches its training baseline. But when confirmed fraud outcomes are compared with the model's predictions, the model quality check shows accuracy falling, because fraudsters now make small, normal-looking purchases. The inputs look the same but mean something different, so the team retrains on recent labeled cases.

cards.definition: Gradual decline in model performance as real-world data changes over time
The ability to describe why a model made a specific prediction
